knowledge_type_note: A tactical motif: a geometric pattern, mechanically detectable, not a guideline. NOTE ON NAMING: 'double attack' was previously listed here as an alias, which the audit flagged as a possible duplicate of the `double-attack` record. They are NOT the same concept in the usage this base follows — a fork is a double attack by ONE piece, while `double-attack` is the general case including discovered attacks. Chess.com merges them; Wikipedia and Chess Tempo do not. The alias has been removed so the distinction is not undermined by the record's own metadata.
definition_short: One piece attacks two or more enemy units at once, so only one can be saved.
definition_long:
A single piece attacks two or more targets simultaneously. The defender can normally answer only one threat, so material falls. Knights fork most often because no other piece attacks a knight back from a forked square, and because the knight's move is the hardest to see. Pawns fork cheaply: the forked pieces being defended does not help, since the pawn is worth less than either.

Forks are ABSOLUTE when one target is the king — the defender is forced to answer the check and cannot save the other piece or insert a zwischenzug (except a cross-check). Otherwise they are RELATIVE, and the defender may have resources: defending both, counter-attacking, or an in-between move.

Targets need not be pieces. A square, a mate threat, or a follow-up fork can be one prong.

history.notes: Tactical motifs are descriptive pattern names of long and mostly anonymous usage. The Chess Informant classification is cited as a standard enumeration, not as the origin of the term.

preconditions: One piece attacks two or more enemy units after the move
indicators_for: At least one target is undefended, or worth more than the forking piece
One target is the king, making the fork absolute
The forking piece is not itself capturable on its square
indicators_against: The forking piece can simply be captured
Both targets are defended and each is worth less than the forker
The defender has a check or a stronger counter-threat available first

typical_moves: A knight to a square attacking king and rook (the classic Nc7+ / Nf7 pattern)
A pawn advance attacking two pieces on adjacent diagonals
A queen check that also picks up a loose piece
tactical_consequences: Wins material when at least one target cannot be saved
strategic_consequences: Loose pieces invite forks; keeping pieces defended is prophylaxis against them

exceptions: A fork wins nothing if the forking piece can be taken, or if every target is adequately defended and cheaper than the forker.
A relative fork can be met by a zwischenzug; an absolute fork cannot.
limitations: Detecting the geometry is mechanical; deciding whether it WINS material requires resolving the whole capture sequence, so recognition alone is not enough.

examples.note: Constructed controlled pair, positive half. Nc7+ forks Ke8 and Ra8; c7 is unguarded because the black bishop stands on e7.

engine.verdict_note: Nc7+ is best at +7.39, a full 2.21 ahead of the next move (Bd3, +5.18). The engine line is 1.Nc7+ Kd7 2.Nxa8 — the rook simply falls. Confirms the motif when the forking square is safe.

examples.note: Real position from the shipped endgame ladder (puzzle en-154023780e). Black plays Re1+, and the point is that the check means the reply is not free — the rook then promotes on d1. Tagged fork by findMotifs() alongside hangingPiece, promotion and zwischenzug, which is a good illustration that several motifs usually co-occur and that ranking them by explanatory importance is the real problem, not detecting them.

engine.verdict_note: Numbers come from the repository's own puzzle verification pipeline at its verdict depth, NOT from education/tools/sf_analyse.py. Recorded that way deliberately so provenance stays honest. The puzzle's stored `why` says the runner-up (Re4) leaves Black losing, so the move is uniquely correct here.

counterexamples.note: Constructed controlled pair, negative half. IDENTICAL to the positive example except the black bishop is on d8 instead of e7, so it guards c7. The fork geometry is unchanged.

engine.verdict_note: Nc7+ collapses to +0.57 and is ranked LAST of the three moves tested, 4.16 behind the best (Bd3, +4.73). The line is 1.Nc7+ Bxc7 — the knight is simply lost. The same geometric pattern swings 6.82 pawns between the two positions purely on whether the forking square is defended. This is the canonical false-match case: geometric detection alone is NOT sufficient to report a fork.

by_level.beginner: This one piece attacks two things at the same time. Your opponent can only save one of them.
by_level.intermediate: A fork. Because it hits {targets} at once and {reason}, the defender cannot cover both.
by_level.advanced: Fork. Note whether it is absolute (a target is the king, so no zwischenzug is available) or relative (the defender may have an in-between resource).

by_depth.short: One piece attacks two things at once.
by_depth.normal: A fork: this piece hits {targets} simultaneously, and only one can be saved. It works because {target} is {undefended / worth more than the forking piece} and the forking square is safe.
by_depth.deep: A single piece attacking two or more targets. It wins material only when at least one target is undefended or outranks the forking piece, and when the forking square itself is safe — those conditions are what separate a fork from a move that merely looks like one. An absolute fork hits the king, so the defender is forced to answer the check and cannot insert a zwischenzug; a relative fork leaves them resources. Targets need not be pieces: a mate threat or a follow-up fork can serve as a prong.
